{{DISPLAYTITLE:Genus ''g'' surface}}
{{short description|Smooth closed surface with g holes}}

In mathematics, a '''genus ''g'' surface''' (also known as a '''''g''-torus''' or '''''g''-holed torus''') is a [[Surface (topology)|surface]] formed by the [[connected sum]] of ''g'' distinct [[torus|tori]]: the interior of a disk is removed from each of ''g'' distinct tori and the boundaries of the ''g'' many disks are identified (glued together), forming a ''g''-torus. The [[genus (mathematics)|genus]] of such a surface is ''g''.

A genus ''g'' surface is a [[two-dimensional]] [[manifold]]. The [[Surface (topology)#Classification of closed surfaces|classification theorem for surfaces]] states that every [[compact space|compact]] [[connected space|connected]] two-dimensional manifold is [[homeomorphism|homeomorphic]] to either the sphere, the connected sum of tori, or the connected sum of [[real projective plane]]s.

==Definition of genus==
{{Main|Genus (mathematics)}}
The genus of a connected orientable surface is an [[integer]] representing the maximum number of cuttings along non-intersecting [[Curve#Topological_curve|closed simple curves]] without rendering the resultant [[manifold]] disconnected.<ref>Munkres, James R. Topology. Vol. 2. Upper Saddle River: Prentice Hall, 2000.</ref> It is equal to the number of [[Handle (mathematics)|handles]] on it. Alternatively, it can be defined in terms of the [[Euler characteristic]] ''χ'', via the relationship ''χ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2&nbsp;−&nbsp;2''g'' for [[Surface_(topology)#Closed_surfaces|closed surfaces]], where ''g'' is the genus. 

The genus (sometimes called the demigenus or Euler genus) of a connected non-orientable closed surface is a positive integer representing the number of [[cross-cap]]s attached to a sphere. Alternatively, it can be defined for a closed surface in terms of the Euler characteristic ''χ'', via the relationship ''χ'' = 2 − ''g'', where ''g'' is the non-orientable genus.

==Genus 0==
An [[orientability|orientable]] surface of genus zero is the [[sphere]] '''''S''<sup>''2''</sup>'''. Another surface of genus zero is the [[disk (mathematics)|disc]].

<gallery class="center" caption="Representations of genus 0 surfaces" widths="150" heights="150" perrow="5">

==Genus 1==
A genus one orientable surface is the ordinary torus. A non-orientable surface of genus one is the [[projective plane]].<ref>{{cite book| first=Glen E. | last=Bredon | author-link=Glen Bredon | title=Topology and Geometry | publisher=Springer-Verlag | year=1993 | isbn=0-387-97926-3}}</ref>

[[Elliptic curve]]s over the [[complex number]]s can be identified with genus 1 surfaces. The formulation of elliptic curves as the embedding of a [[torus]] in the [[complex projective plane]] follows naturally from a property of [[Weierstrass's elliptic functions]] that allows elliptic curves to be obtained from the quotient of the [[complex plane]] by a [[fundamental pair of periods|lattice]].<ref>{{Cite book
 | last = Silverman | first=Joseph H. | author-link=Joseph H. Silverman
 | year = 1986
 | title = The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves
 | series = Graduate Texts in Mathematics
 | volume=106
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | isbn=0-387-96203-4
 }}</ref>

<gallery class="center" caption="Representations of genus 1 surfaces" widths="150" heights="150" perrow="5">
File:Torus illustration.png|A torus of genus 1
File:7_colour_torus.svg|It can be coloured with up to 7 mutually adjacent regions
File:Elliptic curve simple.svg|(Real points of) an elliptic curve
</gallery>

==Genus 2==
The term '''double torus''' is occasionally used to denote a genus 2 surface.<ref>{{MathWorld |title=Double Torus |urlname=DoubleTorus}}</ref><ref name=Mayorga>{{cite journal |last1=Mayorga |first1=Luis S. |last2=Masone |first2=Diego |title=The Secret Ballet Inside Multivesicular Bodies |journal=ACS Nano |date=2024 |volume=18 |issue=24 |pages=15651–15660 |doi=10.1021/acsnano.4c01590|pmid=38830824 }}</ref>
A non-orientable surface of genus two is the [[Klein bottle]].

The [[Bolza surface]] is the most symmetric [[Riemann surface]] of [[Genus (mathematics)|genus]]&nbsp;2, in the sense that it has the largest possible [[conformal map|conformal]] [[automorphism group]].<ref>{{citation|last=Bolza|first= Oskar|title=On Binary Sextics with Linear Transformations into Themselves|journal= American Journal of Mathematics|volume= 10|issue= 1|year= 1887|pages= 47–70|jstor=2369402|doi=10.2307/2369402}}</ref>

<gallery class="center" caption="Representations of genus 2 surfaces" widths="150" heights="150" perrow="5">
File:Double torus illustration.png|A torus of genus 2
File:Tietze_genus_2_colouring.svg|It can be coloured with up to 8 mutually adjacent regions
</gallery>

==Genus 3==
{{for|the three-dimensional space|3-torus}}
The term '''triple torus''' is also occasionally used to denote a genus 3 surface.<ref>{{MathWorld |title=Triple Torus |urlname=TripleTorus}}</ref><ref name="Mayorga" />

The [[Klein quartic]] is a compact [[Riemann surface]] of [[genus (mathematics)|genus]] {{math|3}} with the highest possible order [[automorphism group]] for compact Riemann surfaces of genus 3. It has {{math|168}} orientation-preserving automorphisms, and {{math|336}} automorphisms altogether.
